knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
set.seed(2026)

```{r}
library(RoyAI)
```

## 1. From Roy (1951) to AI adoption

In Roy's model a worker earns $Y_1$ in one sector and $Y_0$ in another and
chooses the better one, $D = 1(Y_1 > Y_0)$. The econometrician sees only
$Y = DY_1 + (1-D)Y_0$, so observed earnings are the outcome of selection.

RoyAI treats AI adoption as the sector choice. Model A is the binary
**generalized Roy model**

$$
Y_s = X'\beta_s + U_s\ (s = 0, 1), \qquad D = 1(Z'\gamma + U_D > 0),
$$

where $D = 1$ marks an AI adopter and $Z$ contains at least one variable
excluded from the outcome equation (an AI cost or access shifter). The
classical Roy model is the special case $Z'\gamma + U_D \propto Y_1 - Y_0$,
and the *extended* Roy model adds an observed cost, $D = 1(Y_1 - Y_0 - W'\pi > 0)$.
All three are fitted by the same likelihood, so they can be tested against each
other.

## 2. Model A on simulated data

`roy_sim_A()` draws from a known data-generating process; the true parameters
are attached to the data.

```{r}
dat <- roy_sim_A(n = 3000, rho0 = -0.3, rho1 = 0.4)
head(dat[, c("y", "d", "x1", "x2", "z")])
fit <- roy(y ~ x1 + x2, d ~ x1 + x2 + z, data = dat)
summary(fit)
```

Compare with the truth:

```{r}
tr <- attr(dat, "truth")
round(cbind(truth = tr, estimate = coef(fit)[names(tr)]), 3)
```

The Heckman two-step estimator, with Murphy-Topel corrected standard errors,
gives a quick check and the starting values for maximum likelihood:

```{r}
fit2 <- roy(y ~ x1 + x2, d ~ x1 + x2 + z, data = dat, method = "twostep")
round(cbind(ml = coef(fit)[1:10], twostep = coef(fit2)[names(coef(fit))[1:10]]), 3)
```

### Treatment parameters

Positive selection on gains ($\rho_1 > 0$, $\rho_0 < 0$) means adopters gain
more from AI than non-adopters would:

```{r}
roy_effects(fit)
c(true_ATE = mean(dat$y1 - dat$y0),
  true_ATT = mean((dat$y1 - dat$y0)[dat$d == 1]),
  true_ATU = mean((dat$y1 - dat$y0)[dat$d == 0]))
```

A naive comparison of adopters and non-adopters mixes the effect with selection:

```{r}
coef(lm(y ~ d + x1 + x2, data = dat))["d"]
```

### Diagnostics

```{r}
roy_diagnostics(fit)
```

## 3. The classical Roy model as a special case

```{r}
dc <- roy_sim_classical(n = 3000, rho01 = 0.3)
f_classical <- roy(y ~ x1 + x2, d ~ x1 + x2, data = dc, type = "classical")
f_general <- suppressWarnings(roy(y ~ x1 + x2, d ~ x1 + x2, data = dc))
roy_lrtest(f_classical, f_general)
```

The test does not reject: on data generated by Roy's rule the restriction
holds. Applied to the AI-adoption data, where costs and other motives drive
selection, it should reject:

```{r}
f_c2 <- roy(y ~ x1 + x2, d ~ x1 + x2 + z, data = dat, type = "extended")
roy_lrtest(f_c2, fit)
```

## 4. Model B: human-only, AI-augmented, AI-dominant

Model B has three production arrangements,
$S = \arg\max_s \{Z'\gamma_s + \varepsilon_s\}$, with an outcome equation for
each. The core estimator is a multinomial logit followed by regime-specific
regressions with Dubin-McFadden correction terms (in the form of
Bourguignon, Fournier and Gurgand, 2007). These terms also identify the
counterfactual means, for example what AI-augmented workers would have earned
in human-only production.

```{r}
db <- roy_sim_B(n = 5000)
table(db$s)
fb <- roy(y ~ x1 + x2, s ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = db)
summary(fb)
roy_effects(fb)
```

```{r}
roy_diagnostics(fb)
```

The correction coefficients are typically imprecise, which the diagnostics
report through the condition numbers of the second-stage designs. Effects on
the treated are better determined than the individual correction terms.

## 5. Plugging in other dependence structures

Each pair $(U_s, U_D)$ is linked by a *dependence family*. The core needs only
the family's conditional distribution function
$h(v \mid u) = P(V \le v \mid U = u)$ on the uniform scale, so a copula
family is added by registering it:

```{r}
frank <- roy_dependence(
  name = "frank_demo", npar = 1L, par_names = "theta",
  h = function(v, u, theta) {
    a <- exp(-theta * u); b <- exp(-theta * v); g <- exp(-theta)
    a * (b - 1) / ((g - 1) + (a - 1) * (b - 1))
  },
  linkinv = function(eta) eta, link = function(theta) theta, start = 1)
roy_register_dependence(frank, overwrite = TRUE)
f_frank <- roy(y ~ x1 + x2, d ~ x1 + x2 + z, data = dat, dependence = "frank_demo")
roy_ic(gaussian = fit, frank = f_frank)
```

The `roy_copula` module registers the Clayton, Gumbel, Frank and Student-t
families (with rotations) in the same way, and `roy_mte` builds marginal
treatment effects on top of `roy_potential()`.

## 5b. Model D: continuous AI-use intensity

AI use is a matter of degree. In Model D intensity `a` in [0, 1) is zero for
non-users and `Lambda(Z'gamma + V)` for users; outcomes are
`Y(a) = mu(x, a) + sigma(a) eps`, and a copula joins `eps` and `V`.
`roy_continuous()` maximises the likelihood of the monograph's Proposition
"Likelihood of Model D", with the same multistart and regularity checks as
Model C.

```{r}
set.seed(10)
dD <- roy_continuous_sim(1500, tau = 0.4)
fitD <- roy_continuous(y ~ x1, a ~ x1 + z1 + z2, data = dD)
fitD
roy_continuous_effects(fitD, a = c(0.2, 0.5), grid = c(0, 0.5), se = FALSE)
```

`TT` is the effect of 0.1 more intensity for workers now at `a`; `TUT` moves
non-users from 0 to `a`.

## 5c. Model E: dynamic selection with learning

In Model E workers do not know their complementarity with AI. They learn it
from AI earnings (Kalman updating) and acquire it by doing at rate `psi`.
`roy_dynamic_solve()` solves the Bellman equation by backward induction;
`roy_dynamic()` estimates the model from a panel by conditional choice
probabilities (`"ccp"`) or nested fixed point (`"nfxp"`).

```{r}
set.seed(11)
pE <- roy_dynamic_sim(500, T = 6, psi = 0.05)
fitE <- roy_dynamic(pE, cost = ~ x, method = "ccp")
fitE
roy_dynamic_effects(fitE)[, c("t", "share_ai", "ATT", "ATU", "option_value_adopters")]
```

The last column is the share of adopters whose expected current net gain is
negative: they try AI for the information and the skills it brings.

## 6. Monte Carlo experiments

`roy_mc()` repeats a simulation and an estimator and reports bias, RMSE and
coverage:

```{r}
mc <- roy_mc(function() roy_sim_A(1000),
             function(d) roy(y ~ x1 + x2, d ~ x1 + x2 + z, data = d, method = "twostep"),
             R = 20, seed = 1)
mc
```

Use `R = 500` or more in research work; `inst/montecarlo-core/mc_core.R`
contains the full design.

## 7. Applied data: PIAAC Cycle 2 and O*NET

`piaac_onet_prep()` turns the PIAAC public-use file and an occupation-level
AI-exposure table into an analysis file. The main exposure measure is the
Felten-Raj-Seamans AI Occupational Exposure index with an occupational
complementarity score; the Eloundou et al. GPT-exposure score is the
robustness check (`exposure_col = "gpt_beta"`). Because PIAAC Cycle 2 is
treated as having no direct AI-use item, adoption is a proxy (AI-exposed
occupation and high ICT use at work), which is a limitation of the applied
work. PUF variable names are resolved from candidate lists and reported, so
they can be checked against the Cycle 2 codebook. The pipeline runs here on
synthetic data:

```{r}
ex <- piaac_example(3000)
pd <- piaac_onet_prep(ex$piaac, ex$exposure)
attr(pd, "notes")
table(pd$s)
pd_gpt <- piaac_onet_prep(ex$piaac, ex$exposure, exposure_col = "gpt_beta")
table(main = pd$s, gpt = pd_gpt$s)
```
